signals.author: Andrey Abakumov
signals.why_relevant: The post discusses building technical talent through entry-level hiring, structured training, and experienced-technician mentorship. This has an adjacent connection to the profile's engineering leadership and multidisciplinary R&D background, but the post focuses on skilled trades, data centers, and infrastructure rather than flight controls, UAVs, robotics, or autonomous systems. The hiring signal is weak and indirect because the author advocates zero-experience hiring without advertising a specific vacancy.
signals.source_text: EVERY COMPANY WANTS EXPERIENCED TECHNICIANS. THE SMART ONES ARE ALSO CREATING THEM. There's a strange cycle happening in the skilled trades. Companies say they can't find enough experienced people. Then another entry-level position gets posted requiring 2 or 3 years of experience. Think about that. Where exactly are those 2 or 3 years supposed to come from? Someone has to be first. Someone has to hire the person who has never worked in a data center. Someone has to teach the person who has never terminated a Cat6 cable. Someone has to show them how to dress cable properly, read prints, label correctly, use a tester and work safely around critical infrastructure. That's why I think companies hiring people into legitimate 0 EXPERIENCE REQUIRED positions deserve more credit. They're taking a risk. Training costs money. Experienced technicians have to spend time teaching. Some new hires won't make it. But the ones who do? That's where things get interesting. Because while everyone else is competing for the same technician with 5 years of experience, you might be developing someone who will become that technician. And there's another part of this we don't talk about enough. Experienced technicians have a huge role in whether this works. Your best technician isn't automatically your best trainer. You need experienced people who remember what it was like to know absolutely nothing. People willing to answer questions. People who correct mistakes without making someone afraid to ask the next question. People who don't treat knowledge like something that needs to be protected. Because the goal isn't simply getting another pair of hands on the project. The goal is turning those hands into a technician. A recent $13 million workforce initiative is expected to support training for more than 5,400 people across 26 states entering skilled trades and infrastructure careers. That's great. But programs alone won't solve the workforce problem. Eventually somebody still has to say: “You don't have experience yet. We'll teach you.” Every experienced technician working today had somebody give them an opportunity before they had the resume they have now. We need more companies willing to do the same. Don't only recruit talent. Build it. If you are a company and you're not connecting with some of the best account managers in the industry to understand what's working for others, you risk falling behind. Look for a partnership and not just someone who is going to hire technicians for you but ACTUALLY care about your companies growth like : Max Kimbarow David Pertosoff Austin Ross Bryan Kincaid Nicholas Pacella The best account managers aren’t just people you talk business with over dinner. They’re the kind of people you build real relationships with, trust, and eventually find yourself inviting to family events. That’s the difference between working with a vendor and building a true partnership.
